problem:
What is the first term that exceeds $58\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
2,\,8,\,32,\,128,\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $58\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.

feedback.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $30$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
2,\,\frac{8}{3},\,\frac{32}{9},\,\frac{128}{27},\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $30$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
feedback.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=2$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{\frac{8}{3}}{2}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $30.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >30 \\ 2\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >30 \\ {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >15 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(15) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(15) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1≈10.413.
$$

Therefore, the $11$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $30.$
